newsitem.title: ROMANIA: ROMANIA SEES GOOD '97 WHEAT CROP, EYES EXPORTS.
newsitem.headline: ROMANIA SEES GOOD '97 WHEAT CROP, EYES EXPORTS.

text.p: Romania hopes to get a good wheat crop this year despite recent heavy rainfalls and floods and plans to re-emerge as a major player on the world grain market, a senior official said on Wednesday.

"Vegetation on 2.3 million hectares of the 2.39 million put under wheat is absolutely remarkable, the best we have had over the past six years," Agriculture Ministry director Matei Georgescu told Reuters.
Georgescu said it was too early to give estimates for the 1997 wheat crop but said the data the ministry had collected so far was "encouraging".

"Our data show that density on the 2.3 million hectares exceeds 400 plants per square metre, which is a very good average for this area. If weather stays fine, we might get a bumper wheat crop and resume exports," Georgescu said.
In 1995, Romania, once a grain basket of Europe, harvested a bumper crop of 7.8 million tonnes and sold over 1.3 million.
Georgescu said the rainfalls and floods which submerged tens of thousands of hectares under wheat over the past weeks had actually been "beneficial" for the 1997 wheat crop.
Ministry data showed last week some 89,000 hectares of farmland were under water or had recorded an "excess of humidity", compared to 18,000 hectares two weeks before.
"The situation is under control now and there are no reasons to worry. The water was drained and humidity in the soil has returned to normal levels," Georgescu said.
Only 18,000 hectares, free of crops, had problems related to excess humidity, data showed.
Meteorologists said on Wednesday wheather would improve across the country over the next days.

Last year, Romania had 2.11 million hectares sown to wheat, but an early winter and late snow damaged the crop on almost half that area. Romania saw its hopes of hard currency earnings from the world grain market shattered.
Romania harvested just 3.1 million tonnes in 1996, some 60 percent down the 1995 level and a record low.
An analyst working for a Western grain trader operating in Romania confirmed the land under wheat looked "good."

"It's true it's towe are behind schedule. But one should have in mind that farmers can resort to seeds with a shorter period of germination, which can solve the problem," Georgescu said, adding that sowing had already started in counties less affected by adverse weather. REUTER
